lesson_title: Your 30 cm Ruler Spans 15 km of South Africa
hook_text: One centimetre of paper is half a kilometre of ground. Your school ruler measures whole districts.
clip_script: Take the ratio literally: one unit of any length on the paper stands for fifty thousand of those same units on the ground. One centimetre on the map is 50 000 centimetres of actual landscape. Now put a size to it: 50 000 centimetres is 500 metres — half a kilometre. On a 1:50 000 sheet, then, each centimetre of paper covers half a kilometre of country, and every two centimetres cover a full kilometre. Lay a ruler across the sheet and you are, quite literally, measuring the landscape. Your standard 30-centimetre ruler, laid across the sheet, is spanning 15 kilometres of real South Africa.
visual_style: Overhead of a topographic sheet with a ruler dropping onto it; each centimetre tick lights up and a matching drone shot counts off half-kilometres of real veld, ending with the whole ruler glowing across 15 km of landscape.
mood: Mind-blown but practical — a superpower hiding in a pencil case.
pacing: Tick-by-tick build along the ruler, quick cut montage of ground shots, big reveal on the 15 km line.
